title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
description: Find the maximum depth of a binary tree using DFS (recursive and iterative) and BFS approaches.

data.text: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its maximum depth. A binary tree's maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.

data.title: TreeNode class

data.text: The depth of a tree is 1 + max(depth of left, depth of right). Recursion naturally explores both subtrees.

data.title: Recursive DFS O(n) — Elegant
Why this works
data.text: Each node visits its children once. The call stack implicitly tracks the path. Time is O(n) because every node is visited once. Space is O(h) where h is tree height (call stack depth).
Use an explicit stack to simulate recursion. Each stack entry carries the node and its depth.

data.title: Iterative DFS O(n) — No recursion
Stack vs recursion
data.text: Iterative DFS uses an explicit stack, giving you control over memory. It's safer for very deep trees where recursion might overflow. The tuple `(node, depth)` tracks state that would otherwise live on the call stack.
BFS processes nodes level by level. We count how many levels we process before the queue empties.

data.title: BFS O(n) — Level counting
BFS insight
data.text: BFS naturally counts levels because we drain the entire queue before incrementing depth. This makes it the most intuitive approach for 'depth of tree' problems, though all three approaches are O(n) time.
